draft.title: Research on neurological disorders
card: A neurological disorder is a condition that affects the nervous system, which includes the brain. Parkinson's disease and epilepsy are two examples.
Researchers study what goes wrong in a disorder and which functions are affected. This shows what the healthy brain does and how its parts work.
movement becomes slow and stiff, and tremor can occur. It is linked to the loss of brain cells that make dopamine, a chemical messenger, so dopamine helps control movement.
sudden bursts of abnormal electrical activity in the brain cause seizures. What a person experiences in a seizure can depend on where in the brain it starts.
draft.remember: Studying what goes wrong in a disorder can show what a healthy brain does.

a.q: How can research on Parkinson's disease add to what is known about the brain?
opts: Loss of dopamine cells links to movement control
It shows the brain does not change after birth
It proves all movement is controlled by one lobe
It shows dopamine has no role in the brain
a.why: Parkinson's disease involves the loss of dopamine-making cells and problems with movement. This suggests dopamine helps control movement. The other options claim things that the card does not support.
a.clue: Think about what is lost and what function is affected.

b.q: Researchers find that one person's seizures always begin in one small brain area, and the person feels the same unusual sensation at the start of each seizure. What does this suggest?
opts: That area may be involved in that sensation
That epilepsy is caused by a lack of dopamine
That the seizure shows the whole brain is damaged
That the sensation has no link to any brain area
b.why: What a person experiences in a seizure can depend on where it starts. So a repeated sensation from one starting area suggests that area helps produce that sensation. Epilepsy is linked to abnormal electrical activity, not to dopamine loss, which belongs to Parkinson's disease.
b.clue: Where a seizure starts can shape what the person experiences.

a.best: Loss of dopamine cells links to movement control

b.best: That area may be involved in that sensation

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the only one not phrased as 'It shows/proves...', and the three distractors are extreme absolutes ('no role', 'does not change', 'all movement... one lobe'). A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may be involved'). The other three are absolute claims ('caused by', 'no link', 'whole brain is damaged'), so the answer can be picked by elimination of extremes alone.

proposal.title: Research on neurological disorders
card: A neurological disorder is a condition that affects the nervous system, which includes the brain. Parkinson's disease and epilepsy are two examples.
Researchers study what goes wrong in a disorder and which functions are affected. This shows what the healthy brain does and how its parts work.

movement becomes slow and stiff, and tremor can occur. These movement problems come from the loss of brain cells that make dopamine, a chemical messenger. This suggests dopamine helps control movement.
sudden bursts of abnormal electrical activity in the brain cause seizures. What a person experiences in a seizure can depend on where in the brain it starts.
proposal.remember: Studying what goes wrong in a disorder can show what a healthy brain does.

a.q: How can research on Parkinson's disease add to what is known about the brain?
opts: It suggests dopamine helps the brain control movement
It suggests dopamine mainly helps the brain process sight
It suggests slow movement makes dopamine cells die off
It suggests seizures start when dopamine cells are lost
a.why: In Parkinson's disease, dopamine-making cells are lost and movement problems follow. This suggests dopamine helps control movement. The idea that slow movement kills the cells reverses cause and effect: the cell loss comes first.
a.clue: Think about what is lost and which function is then affected.

b.q: Researchers find that one person's seizures always begin in one small brain area, and the person feels the same unusual sensation at the start of each seizure. What does this suggest?
opts: That area may help produce that particular sensation
The sensation may be what causes the seizure to start
That area may have lost its dopamine-making cells
Every brain area may produce that sensation equally
b.why: What a person experiences in a seizure can depend on where it starts, so a repeated sensation from one starting area suggests that area helps produce it. The sensation does not cause the seizure: seizures are caused by bursts of abnormal electrical activity. Loss of dopamine cells belongs to Parkinson's disease, not epilepsy.
b.clue: Where a seizure starts can shape what the person experiences.

b.best: That area may help produce that particular sensation
